  label: Describing your ABI

import { Aside, CardGrid, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Your app's **ABI** is a machine-readable description of everything it exposes:
its methods with their argument and return types, the events it emits, and the
shape and version of its persistent state.
It ships with the code, embedded in the compiled wasm.

Three consumers read it.
A caller - `meroctl`, a frontend, any client - reads `methods` to build a
correctly typed request and decode the reply without ever seeing your Rust.
A code generator reads the same entries to emit a typed client.
And the node reads it on **upgrade**: the state portion is what the
no-silent-downgrade rail and the migration replay compare between the installed
version and the new one, so an ABI that describes the wrong state shape is not a
documentation bug, it is a wrong migration plan.

This page is about how that description is produced from your code.
For the manifest's field-by-field format, see
[App interface (ABI)](/build/app-abi/).

## Every type describes itself

There is no schema file to maintain and nothing parses your source.
Each type that can appear in an ABI position implements the `AbiType` trait,
which answers two questions: how a use site refers to the type, and what named
definition (if any) it contributes to the manifest.
Because the compiler picks the impls, an alias is already the aliased type, a
re-export resolves to its definition, and a macro-generated type has already
expanded by the time it is asked to describe itself.

The SDK covers everything you do not own - the std scalars and collections, the
CRDT collections from `calimero-storage`, and the id types (`AccountId`,
`ContextId`, `BlobId`, `PublicKey`).
Your own types are covered like this:

| Item | Where its `AbiType` impl comes from |
|------|-------------------------------------|
| `#[app::state]` struct | derived for you by the attribute |
| `#[app::event]` enum | derived for you by the attribute |
| any other struct or enum in a method signature, an event payload, or a state field | one line: `#[derive(AbiType)]` |

```rust
use calimero_sdk::abi::AbiType;

#[derive(AbiType)]
pub struct Profile {
    display_name: Option<String>,
    joined_at: u64,
}
```

`#[app::private]` is deliberately absent from that table: node-local state is
never synchronized and never described.

## From the derive to the wasm

`#[app::logic]` generates a hidden `__calimero_abi()` that walks those impls and
assembles the manifest.
It is `cfg`-gated and compiled in only when the toolchain asks for it, which a
wasm build never does - so **your bytecode is unaffected**, and an app pays
nothing at runtime for describing itself.

`cargo mero build` extracts the manifest by compiling and running that entry
point **on the host**, writes it to `res/abi.json`, and embeds a canonicalized
copy into the wasm as the `calimero_abi_v1` custom section.
The section is part of the module's bytes, so it is covered by the blob's
content hash and cannot drift from the code it describes.
See [the cargo mero toolchain](/build/cargo-mero/) for the rest of the pipeline.

## What you actually do

Usually nothing.
State and events are covered by their own attributes and every SDK and std type
already describes itself, so `#[derive(AbiType)]` is for the auxiliary structs
and enums you introduce.

Forget one and it is a compile error naming the type, not a silent gap in the
manifest:

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `Profile: AbiType` is not satisfied
   |            ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `AbiType` is not implemented for `Profile`
```

The fix is the derive.
With it, the `Profile` above lands in the manifest's `types` as:

```json
"Profile": {
  "kind": "record",
  "fields": [
    { "name": "display_name", "nullable": true, "type": { "kind": "string" } },
    { "name": "joined_at", "type": { "kind": "u64" } }
  ]
}
```

Note what happened to `Option<String>`: the described type is the unwrapped
`string`, and the optionality rides a `nullable` flag on the field, while a
non-optional field carries no `nullable` key at all.
The same rule applies to parameters and returns, so a client reads nullability
off the position rather than off the type.

## Naming

A type's manifest name defaults to its Rust identifier.
`#[abi(name = "...")]` overrides it:

```rust
#[derive(AbiType)]
#[abi(name = "UserProfile")]
pub struct Profile {
    display_name: Option<String>,
    joined_at: u64,
}
```

A name is the manifest's only handle on a type, so two different shapes may not
share one.
If they do, the build fails during extraction with:

```
ABI type name collision: Profile defined with two different shapes.
```

There are two ways out, depending on what actually collided:

- **Two distinct types with the same identifier**, say a `Profile` in two
  modules. Give one of them a different manifest identity with
  `#[abi(name = "...")]`; the Rust names stay as they are.
- **One generic used at two argument types.** A generic is described at its
  instantiation under its bare identifier, so `Wrapper<String>` and
  `Wrapper<u64>` both want to be `Wrapper`. Define a separate concrete type per
  instantiation so every shape has its own name.

## Constraining a newtype

A one-field tuple struct describes as an alias to its inner type.
`#[abi(pattern = "...")]` records what its values are allowed to look like:

```rust
#[derive(AbiType)]
#[abi(pattern = "^[0-9a-f]{64}$")]
pub struct FolderId(String);
```

The pattern is ECMA-262 source text and lands on the alias in the manifest:

```json
{ "kind": "alias", "target": { "kind": "string" }, "pattern": "^[0-9a-f]{64}$" }
```

It is **descriptive, not enforced**.
The node does not check values against it; a generated client uses it to reject
bad input at its own boundary, before a call goes out.
Whatever the app itself requires still has to be checked in the app.

`pattern` applies only to a one-field tuple struct.
On anything else the build fails, because there is no single value for it to
describe:

```
`pattern` applies only to a one-field tuple struct
```

## Doc comments

Your `///` comments ship in the ABI.
A method, parameter, type, field, enum variant, or event with a doc comment carries it as `doc`, so a client or an agent can learn what a method is for without your source.
An item without a comment has no `doc` key, and editing a comment is never an ABI change: `cargo mero abi diff` ignores it.
The comment is still embedded in the wasm, so a doc-only edit produces different bytes and a new blob hash.

Rust does not allow `///` on a parameter, so parameters use rustdoc's `# Arguments` list:

```rust
/// Apply a batch of block edits.
///
/// # Arguments
/// * `edits` - at most 512 per call.
/// * `now` - caller's unix seconds; orders concurrent
///   edits (last writer wins).
///
/// # Errors
/// Fails if more than 512 edits are sent in one call.
pub fn set_blocks(&mut self, edits: Vec<Edit>, now: u64) -> app::Result<u32>
```

Each entry becomes that parameter's `doc` and the section is removed from the method's own `doc`; `# Errors`, `# Examples`, and any other section except `# Returns` stay.
An indented line continues the entry above it, and a blank line ends it.
Every other line in the section fails the build, so it cannot vanish from the ABI unnoticed: an unindented wrapped line, a paragraph after a blank line, a numbered list, or intro prose.
Put such text above the `# Arguments` heading instead.

```
`# Arguments` line "Must be positive." must be an entry like * `name` - description, or be indented to continue one
```

An entry that names something other than a parameter fails the build:

```
`# Arguments` names `edit`, which is not a parameter of `set_blocks`
```

So does naming the same parameter twice:

```
`# Arguments` names `edits` more than once in `set_blocks`
```

A `# Returns` section becomes the method's `returns_doc` and is removed from its `doc`.
A method whose success value is unit, including one returning `app::Result<()>`, has nothing to describe, so a `# Returns` on it fails the build; document its failures under `# Errors` instead.

Two attributes tell callers how careful to be, and are recorded on the method:

```rust
/// Remove a board and every element on it.
#[app::destructive]
#[app::idempotent]
pub fn delete_board(&mut self, id: String) -> app::Result<()>
```

`#[app::destructive]` means the call removes data (clear, remove, delete, unregister); updating or overwriting a caller-supplied value is never destructive. `#[app::idempotent]` means repeating it with the same arguments changes nothing further.
They are hints for clients and agents, not enforced by the node, and a method may carry both.
Either one on a read-only method or on `init` fails the build.

## Serde attributes

The ABI describes the JSON your app actually sends and receives, so `derive(AbiType)` reads your `#[serde(...)]` attributes.
`rename`, `rename_all`, `rename_all_fields`, `skip`, `tag`, `content` and `untagged` are reflected in the manifest.
`default`, `skip_serializing_if`, `alias`, `deny_unknown_fields`, `bound`, `borrow` and `crate` do not change the shape and are accepted.

An attribute whose effect the ABI cannot describe fails the build instead of producing a wrong manifest: `flatten`, `transparent`, `from`/`into`/`try_from`, `other`, the one-direction `skip_serializing`/`skip_deserializing`, and the `rename(serialize = .., deserialize = ..)` forms.

A field written by your own function (`with`, `serialize_with`, `deserialize_with`) has to say what it writes:

```rust
#[derive(AbiType, Serialize)]
pub struct FileRecord {
    #[serde(serialize_with = "serialize_blob_id_hex")]
    #[abi(as = String)]
    pub blob_id: [u8; 32],
}
```

## Inspecting the ABI

`cargo mero abi` reads a compiled module or the artifacts beside it:

```bash
cargo mero abi extract res/my_app.wasm --output abi.json  # the full manifest
cargo mero abi types res/my_app.wasm                      # just the named types
cargo mero abi state res/my_app.wasm                      # state root + its dependencies
cargo mero abi inspect res/my_app.wasm                    # the wasm's sections
cargo mero abi diff res/state-schema.json baseline.json   # breaking + unsafe changes
```

`diff` is the one worth wiring into CI.
It applies the same classification the node's upgrade gate does, flagging a
breaking field change and, more importantly, an unsafe identity downgrade - an
`AuthoredMap`, `AuthoredVector`, or `SharedStorage` field replaced by a plain
type, which silently strips per-entry authorship or the writer ACL.
Catching that before a release is much cheaper than after an install.

<Aside type="caution" title="Known limitations">
- **A `#[cfg]` on a logic method still lands in the ABI.** An attribute macro
  sees your item before `cfg` is applied, so a method gated out of an
  `#[app::logic]` block is still described and the manifest advertises a method
  the wasm may not export. The same holds for a gated variant of an
  `#[app::event]` enum. (A gated *struct field* is fine: that description comes
  from a derive, which runs after `cfg` is applied.) Express a variant as whole
  gated items instead - see
  [cargo mero's feature docs](/build/cargo-mero/).
- **Gate on features, not on the target.** Extraction compiles on the host, so
  an ABI-visible item gated on `target_arch` describes its *host* form rather
  than its wasm one. Features are shared between extraction and the wasm build;
  the target is not.
- **Do not gate ABI-visible items on `cfg(test)`.** Extraction runs through the
  test harness, so a test-gated field or type would be described even though the
  shipped wasm omits it (and it would break borsh parity between test and
  production builds anyway).
- **An older SDK produces no ABI at all.** An app whose SDK predates
  `__calimero_abi` builds no manifest, so `cargo mero build` warns, writes no
  `res/abi.json` or `res/state-schema.json`, and embeds no section. The wasm is
  still produced, but `cargo mero bundle` refuses it, because every bundle entry
  names an `abi.json`.
</Aside>
